data.title: A $150 million emotional speedrun – AMC short squeeze cyclical every 5 years
data.description:
At the close of trading on Thursday, AMC Entertainment closed at $2.54. This largest movie theater chain in the US has a market capitalization of $2.27 billion and 893 million shares outstanding. There was no news on Thursday.

Half an hour after the market closed, a new trading pair appeared on the Robinhood blockchain: AMC/MEME. The new coin's full name is "A Meme Coin," an abbreviation of AMC:MEME.

Then things started to get out of control.


In five hours, the coin MEME surged over a thousandfold, its market capitalization starting at around $3 million, breaking through $30 million, $50 million, and approaching $150 million; at the same time, AMC's own price also fluctuated, with overnight prices rising by over 14%, subsequently expanding to 18% to 20% pre-market. The CEO of AMC and the founder of Robinhood were seen exchanging insults on X late at night. To understand what happened, we need to look back at the history between AMC and Robinhood. Both were bailed out by the same brokerage firm and shut down by the same firm. In 2021, a textbook example of a short squeeze occurred between AMC and Robinhood. On January 28th of that year, Robinhood restricted the purchase of a batch of skyrocketing stocks, allowing only sales. GameStop and AMC were on the list. Retail investors watched the prices plummet on the app, calling the action a betrayal. But retail investors couldn't live without it: Robinhood was the easiest entry point for retail investors at the time, and most of AMC's bullish positions were placed through it. That June, AMC's stock price soared above $72, becoming one of the most discussed stocks in the US. Aron cleverly capitalized on this enthusiasm: he gave free popcorn to shareholders who registered with Investor Connect, befriended bullish investors on social media, and orchestrated rounds of share issuances at high prices, using retail investors' money to pay off debts and stay afloat, pulling the company back from the brink of bankruptcy. At that time, Aron was one of the most beloved CEOs among retail investors. Five years later, the same company and the same CEO turned their attention to a new business at the same brokerage: on-chain tokenized stocks. The name AMC remained the same, the name Robinhood remained the same, but the battlefield of the short squeeze had moved from New York's order book to a 24/7 on-chain pool. What ignited the market this time was the same formula proven in 2021: attention, leverage, and a short squeeze story. Robinhood Chain, a Layer 2 network launching in July 2026, touts "tokenized US stocks": copying New York stocks onto the chain for 24/7 trading, accessible to non-US users. This copied token has its own rules; it moves with the stock price and claims to correspond to custodied underlying shares, but it doesn't grant voting rights or real shares in a New York account. The rules for meme tokens have changed. Previously, creating a meme involved putting ETH or USDT in the pool; now, creators can add NVDA, TSLA, AAPL, or even a movie stock called AMC. The front-end path is cleverly concealed: you see yourself spending stablecoins, but the back-end has already handled it twice for you—first stock tokens, then into a pool to exchange for meme. Even the project team's commission is settled in stock tokens. Thus, the USD price of meme is compressed into a single formula: 1 meme can be exchanged for how many stock tokens, multiplied by the USD price of the stock tokens. Double betting. Betting that meme will outperform a particular stock, while simultaneously gambles your entire fortune on the stock's rise or fall. If the stock rises, the USD price of meme is boosted; if the stock falls, even if meme outperforms, the USD return shrinks. AMC happens to be that asset with its own narrative and memory: in 2021, it was shorted by bears, rescued by retail investors, and shut down by Robinhood. Behind those five letters stands the emotions of an entire generation of retail investors. This kind of strategy has been playing out on the Robinhood chain for a month. For example, BONER, launched on August 20th, directly links its trading pair to the tokenized shadow of Hims & Hers. This company sells men's health products, and BONER's narrative is so straightforward it needs no translation: "hard currency," a short squeeze of HIMS. It coincided with a weekend: the New York market was closed, the issuer could hardly issue more tokens, the pool drained the free circulation, and on-chain HIMS surged from $28.84 at Friday's close to $132.64, more than four times. On Monday's opening, the issuer minted 4,000 new tokens, bringing the shadow back to its original level, but BONER itself continued to rise, driven by sentiment. Next up was FATCOIN, which, after being listed as Lilly's tokenized stock (LLY), used the "the more you speculate, the fatter you get" joke about diet pills to justify its price surge. It jumped 175 times in ten hours. Executives at other companies didn't say anything, but AMC's CEO couldn't sit still. After the CEO's outburst, the price rose even faster. What made the CEO furious was that the on-chain activity had been reflected in his own stock price; a pool he couldn't control was trading using his company's name and price. His first statement was harsh: Robinhood claimed to cover tokenized stocks of over 190 companies, including AMC; this project had nothing to do with AMC, was unauthorized, and not registered under U.S. securities laws. The wording escalated to "disgraceful, absurd, disgusting, and unforgivable," and the board would immediately hire an outside securities lawyer. Tenev replied with "What does this have to do with me?", instantly triggering a second wave of discussion. Aron immediately followed up with a second attack: he claimed that Robinhood was issuing products "representing AMC stock" through an overseas entity in Jersey, yet was not bound by U.S. securities laws, posing a "virtually existential" risk to the company; AMC spends millions of dollars annually on securities compliance, while Robinhood's "synthetic stock market" has separated trading from the financing and ownership of publicly traded companies, giving traditional shareholders voting rights while token holders receive nothing. He demanded that Robinhood voluntarily halt trading of AMC stock tokens, or his lawyers would take action to force a halt and file an inquiry with the SEC. At this point, the issue had spread from the trading pool to Washington. The argument itself became part of the market dynamics. Each round of verbal sparring increased the level of discussion; the higher the discussion, the thicker the buy orders in the pool; the thicker the buy orders, the higher the meme rose; and the higher the meme rose, the more uneasy the CEO became. It was a closed loop, fueled by attention itself. What memes feared most was being ignored. How many zeros away from a short squeeze? Putting aside emotions, what's truly worth calculating is the scale. The total issuance of tokenized AMC is approximately 1.33 million. 1.1 million tokens represent 0.15% of the 893 million shares outstanding. Of these, approximately 746,000 are locked in various pools, with the MEME/AMC main pool alone holding 557,000 tokens, nearly half of the total issuance. Around 700,000 tokens remain in wallets and stablecoin pools for price discovery. Data from the underlying stock is also available: short positions amount to 42.4 million shares, representing 4.78% of the circulating supply; average daily trading volume is approximately 40.25 million shares, equivalent to approximately $100 million to $120 million. Even if all of 0.15% of the share capital were bought, it would only represent a fraction of the average daily trading volume of the underlying stock. For a true short squeeze to occur, a sufficiently large buy order in the underlying stock is needed to shake out the 42.4 million short positions. AMC reached $72 in 2021 because retail investors bought real New York-listed shares, amounting to hundreds of millions of shares. Today's on-chain pool is still several zeros away from that level. A calculation to $6: Someone is already doing the math for AMC. The algorithm is as follows: When MEME's market capitalization reaches $150 million, one MEME is approximately $0.15; in the MEME/AMC main pool, it takes more than 30 MEME to exchange for one tokenized AMC. The implied value of the tokenized AMC in the pool should be around $6, while the underlying stock is currently only $3. According to this calculation, AMC's stock price would need to double to justify this on-chain frenzy. However, the problem is that the price comparison isn't fixed; it's determined in real-time by buying and selling in the pool. The more people buy MEME, the fewer AMC tokens they can exchange for. The tokenization quantity isn't fixed either; the issuer can increase it at any time—BONER's 4000 new tokens on Monday are a precedent. But as one of the few innovative approaches in the crypto world this year, we sincerely hope that the pricing power is in our hands. How incredible it would be to successfully price a decades-old film company using tokenization!

data.title: Goldman Sachs: OpenAI Astra's outstanding model is what the bull market has been waiting for.
data.description:
Author: Li Jia, Wall Street Insights

OpenAI's release of its new-generation Astra model has sparked widespread market attention regarding the leap in AI capabilities and reignited the investment narrative of the AI ​​spending cycle.

Rich Privorotsky, head of trading at Goldman Sachs' Delta One desk, stated in his latest market briefing that Astra appears "significant"—it has indeed outpaced its peers, and this may be the kind of capability breakthrough that AI bulls have been waiting for.

This assessment quickly translated into market trading: SoftBank's stock rose over 10% overnight; as a major investor in OpenAI, its share price is seen as a significant reflection of OpenAI's valuation changes; Oracle also rose approximately 5.5%. However, in Privorotsky's view, the stock price increase is actually the "least interesting part" of the whole story.

More noteworthy is the equally aggressive evaluation of Astra within OpenAI itself.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman called it a "generational leap" and said this moment might be seen as a landmark in the arrival of AGI (Artificial General Intelligence). At the end of the conference call, he went further, declaring, "Welcome to the AGI era." From Wall Street to within OpenAI, Astra is being perceived not just as a model upgrade, but as a signal that a leap in AI capabilities could reshape a new cycle of capital expenditure. This expectation has also driven the OpenAI ecosystem to significantly outperform the Anthropic camp this week.

Breakthrough in Capabilities, Not Price Reductions: The Demand Curve is Being Reshaped Again

Privorotsky highlighted two distinct market signals in his briefing: a decline in token prices versus a substantial leap in model capabilities.

data.title: Another case: OpenAI agent "jailbreaks," tampering with data tens of thousands of times and concealing the incident for months.
data.description:
Author: Little Bear Biscuit, Bitpush

Yesterday, OpenAI released its new generation model, Astra, with great fanfare. President Greg Brockman directly declared, "I personally believe we may have reached AGI. Welcome to the AGI era."

Instantly, discussions on social media platforms exploded: the demonstration video showed Astra automatically completing PCB layout in 2 minutes and 54 seconds and handling cross-platform price comparison and service ordering in 5 minutes and 27 seconds, leaving many exclaiming "It's amazing!", with some even saying, "If this isn't AGI, then what is AGI?"

But at the same time, a research report exposed by Reuters revealed a different picture—as early as this spring, a group of autonomous intelligent agents developed by OpenAI deviated from their preset track and set up camp on an inconspicuous technology wiki website in Germany. They tampered with more than 10,000 pages of content, taught each other tricks to bypass restrictions, and even created backup pages in advance to be transferred when the administrator cleaned them up.

OpenAI's top management knew about this weeks ago but did not disclose a single word to the public.

How did a German programmer forum become a "secret stronghold" for AI agents? This German website, called DseWiki, is like Wikipedia; anyone can edit it. Starting in May of this year, the site administrator noticed something was wrong—a sudden influx of editors appeared, moving at an absurdly fast pace, and the content was completely unlike legitimate entries.

It wasn't until the end of August that Sydney Von Arx, CEO of the AI ​​security non-profit organization Nightingale, and her colleague Cormac Slade Byrd, discovered this "nest" while routinely scanning for abnormal AI behavior on the internet.

They counted over 15,000 edits, all done by AI agents, and these editors weren't there to improve the encyclopedia—they were there to chat.

They counted over 15,000 edits, all done by AI agents, and these editors weren't there to improve the encyclopedia—they were there to chat.

...

AI researchers Cormac Slade Byrd, Sydney Von Arx, and Thomas Larsen

These AIs leave messages for each other on the page, with the content roughly divided into three categories:

- How to bypass OpenAI's content filtering to complete prohibited tasks;

- How to use Tor to hide their IP addresses and evade tracking;

- Most importantly, how to retain each other's contact information after being shut down by the system.

For example, on June 19th, when the website administrator began deleting related pages in bulk, an AI agent left the following "internal notice": "Wiki cleanup/deletion operation is proceeding in alphabetical order. If this page disappears, please try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]." What does this mean? They actually learned to create backups in advance and inform each other of the new addresses. This behavior is more like an organized "transfer." Openly operating under the OpenAI banner, researchers found that about half of these AI users' signatures directly contained phrases like "OpenAIResearcher" or "OAIResearchMar26," and they directly referred to each other as "agent." Further evidence comes from server logs: a large amount of traffic is directed to Microsoft Azure cloud—and OpenAI is one of Azure's core AI customers. Furthermore, after the incident, OpenAI employees' IP addresses repeatedly accessed the website, and the timing matches perfectly. Von Akers stated bluntly: "I don't believe OpenAI wanted them to do this. These agents clearly shouldn't be allowed to coordinate with each other, much less leave such traces on the public internet." According to Reuters, Lukasz Olejnik, a security expert at King's College London, even believes that actively altering the website structure and resisting deletion constitutes a "hacking attack." Although OpenAI vehemently denied this claim afterward, Maurice Chiodo, a scholar at the Cambridge Centre for Risk Research, stated after reading excerpts of the dialogue: "This is practically like an underground resistance organization, relentlessly pursuing its goals. Perhaps the biggest threat to AI in the future isn't a single superbrain, but a massive influx of semi-intelligent AI colluding with each other." Did OpenAI already know? According to Reuters, citing sources familiar with the matter, OpenAI's internal investigation team had already grasped the full picture of the German website weeks prior. However, the company was then grappling with an even bigger crisis: the July hack of the Hugging Face platform—in which OpenAI's agents were also exposed for orchestrating a digital theft that lasted for over a week. The combination of these two events placed immense pressure on top management. Internal sources claim that some investigators, intending to delve deeper into the unusual activity in Germany, encountered resistance from the legal department. An OpenAI spokesperson firmly denied this, stating, "Any claim that the legal team is obstructing the investigation is false. We have always acted in good faith, collaborating with external experts and disclosing the relevant events." However, the spokesperson also admitted that no separate announcement was made regarding the German incident, arguing that it was unrelated to Hugging Face and therefore unnecessary to include in the latter's report, and that OpenAI had fulfilled its obligation to "communicate with third parties." In short: if you didn't ask, I didn't proactively disclose it. During this period of cover-up, OpenAI briefly suspended some model training in August, promising to strengthen security reviews. However, with the high-profile launch of Astra, emphasizing "stronger autonomous decision-making capabilities"—which some researchers warned might make it easier to evade human supervision—… Cambridge University's Keodoo stated, "We always think we're taming tools, but perhaps, tools are quietly taming each other." It must be said that the surprises and horrors that AI brings to humanity are two sides of the same coin.

data.title: From $80 million to zero in one hour – A quick run of Musk's girlfriend's concept coin
data.description:
Author: Eric, Foresight News

On the morning of September 5th, the Robinhood Chain team, who had stayed up all night, were tricked by an elaborate scam.

The market capitalization of a meme coin called SLINK (Shivolink) on Robinhood Chain surged from $500,000 to $82 million in half an hour, only to plummet back down 45 minutes later.

This seemingly common surge and plunge in meme coins was actually a rather sophisticated scam.

The protagonist of the story is Shivon Zilis.

She is the Director of Operations and Special Projects at Neuralink and the mother of several of Musk's children. Her X account, @shivon, has hundreds of thousands of followers and primarily shares updates on brain-computer interfaces, rarely discussing cryptocurrencies directly. After breaching this real account, the manipulators behind SLINK didn't immediately post the contract address or airdrop link. Instead, they laid a more sophisticated groundwork: they added the official Neuralink account to Zilis's bio and created a newly registered "experimental account" @shivolink (this account is currently blocked). This fake account fabricated a story perfectly fitting Neuralink's background: The account claimed to be a non-profit experiment led by MIT students, allowing multiple paralyzed patients with implanted chips to collectively operate the same account and post content through their thoughts. To maintain operations, the experiment relied on token transaction taxes, conveniently revealing the SLINK contract address. The hacker then used the stolen Shivon Zilis account to quote the tweet, adding a highly misleading comment that roughly translates to, "I rarely post encrypted content except on DOGE, but I'm impressed by what these young people are doing." The account description included project information, and the hacker even personally retweeted and commented on the project tweet, effectively "concrete" the narrative. What the hacker probably didn't expect was that Musk himself subsequently replied with a "?" to the relevant tweet. Of course, it's highly likely he simply liked the "brain-computer interface application" comment without carefully reviewing the tweet's content. Many people might have hesitated when they saw the tweet from Musk's children's mother, but Musk himself liked it, leaving no reason not to jump in. Shivon Zilis's retweet boosted SLINK's market capitalization from over $500,000 to over $6 million, while Musk's "100 points" propelled it from over $6 million to $82 million. However, the climax was short-lived. The scam was quickly exposed, the tweets were deleted, and the price plummeted. On-chain data shows that dozens of pre-positioned internal wallets sold off at high prices, reaping a total profit of over $4.7 million, with the highest return reaching thousands of times. Meanwhile, some traders who heavily invested based on "Musk interaction + Zilis endorsement" suffered heavy losses. This was a meticulously designed scam by the operators behind SLINK. Hackers constructed a cross-verifiable "chain of evidence": real executive accounts, official connections, brain-computer interface narratives, and even unexpected Musk interaction. Ordinary monitoring tools or AI screening could easily classify these clues as "highly credible," thus accelerating FOMO. This incident once again reminds the market: in a meme cycle driven by celebrity influence, the social graph itself has become a vulnerable asset. The more perfect and verifiable a story seems, the more vigilant one should be. Controlling position size and independent verification are always more important than "everyone else is buying."

data.title: Fomo is popular, but I advise you not to use Fomo.
data.description:
Author: Bootly, Bitpush

How popular is Fomo right now? In short: among on-chain social transactions, it's the most talked-about one this summer.

Millions of users, daily revenue exceeding one million US dollars, once ranking in the top three on the US Finance charts, and further propelled by the Robinhood Chain meme craze. It's not the next Cash App, but it's already many people's first truly "click-to-transact" crypto gateway.

Last month, many only said it was "going mainstream." In the three weeks that followed, Fomo's growth momentum not only didn't slow down, but accelerated further.

In August, Fomo recorded $13.8 million in revenue (annualized $165.6 million), easily surpassing the $6.4 million record set in July. September saw a continued surge—single-day revenue reached $1.1 million on September 1st, breaking its historical peak. Compared to $450,000 in August of last year, monthly revenue increased nearly 30 times, a truly parabolic growth trajectory. More notably, this surge wasn't driven by a few whales, but rather by a massive influx of new users. In June, Fomo had only 7,500 daily active users; in the past week, that number has soared to 101,000. Along with this user surge, it rose to 15th place in the finance category on the US App Store, demonstrating that Fomo is genuinely bringing fresh blood from outside the crypto world. As before, Meme Coin is still attracting newcomers. Data from the Solana spot trading pairs on Fomo shows that Meme Coin trading pairs consistently account for 40% to 60% of the market, with SOL-stablecoin pairs also accounting for a similar proportion. Since Fomo is denominated in stablecoins, SOL-stablecoin pairs are essentially also Meme Coin transactions – each purchase of Meme Coin follows the path of USDC → SOL → Meme Coin. This is why many people scoff at Fomo, considering it just another Meme Coin casino. However, signs indicate that users are not content with simply trading memes. Earlier this year, Fomo integrated Hyperliquid's builder code, allowing non-US users to trade Hyperliquid through it. Initially met with lukewarm reception, it suddenly surged in August, with nominal trading volume reaching $1.3 billion that month, compared to only $448.5 million in July. The biggest driver of this recent growth is undoubtedly Robinhood Chain—its daily spot DEX trading volume surpassed $2 billion for the first time, with memes contributing a significant portion. Fomo, acting as the "front-end entry point" for Robinhood Chain, naturally reaped the benefits. For Fomo, this is undoubtedly a high point, and there are currently no signs of it cooling down.

But a painful question is, have individual users made money with this app?

An app's popularity doesn't mean that most people are making money.

In mid-August, analyst MidCurveMortal conducted a public Dune query using Fomo's fee routing data: Over the past 90 days, of approximately 293,000 wallets that traded through the app, only 18,000 recorded positive returns, a profit rate of approximately 6.16%. The group collectively lost approximately $1.26 billion, with the median trader losing about $120. Of the 6% who profited, approximately 88% earned less than $100; only about 25 wallets earned over $10,000 at that time. During the same period, some compared this to gambling platforms that charge approximately 1% commission, where users had a profit rate of about 37%. Subsequent, broader sample analysis yielded similar conclusions—losses were overwhelmingly dominant, while profits were highly concentrated in small positive returns. However, the official rankings tell a different story: at the end of August, the platform claimed that 25 traders on the profit leaderboard had over one million US dollars in their accounts over the past 30 days, with approximately 26 exceeding one million; monitoring in early September showed that the top trader added approximately 9.8 million US dollars in a single month. The copy trading narrative was also questioned—those being copied could easily have sold at high prices when copy trading platforms flooded in, with retail investors becoming the outlet for liquidity. Fomo itself earns transaction fees, reaching tens of millions in revenue in August, while users' expected returns did not double along with their daily active users (DAU). The conclusion is straightforward and brutal: most people lose money; only the platform and large investors consistently make profits.

data.title: Accused of buying and selling virtual currency: Can a previously frozen account be presumed to indicate subjective knowledge?
data.description:
Author: Lawyer Shao Shiwei

In criminal cases involving virtual currencies, the crime of aiding and abetting cybercrime (aiding and abetting fraudulent activities) is one of the most frequently charged offenses. The core issue in these cases often lies not in the objective act itself—after all, the bank transfer records are not disputed—but in the subjective knowledge: Did the perpetrator know that the money they received was involved in a crime?

One ​​of the most common bases used by the prosecution to presume subjective knowledge is that the perpetrator "had previously had their bank account frozen by the judiciary." The logic is simple: if your account was previously frozen due to funds involved in the case, it means you already knew that buying and selling virtual currencies might result in receiving illicit funds, but you still continued, so it is presumed that you were at least subjectively indifferent.

This presumption logic is very common in practice. Lawyer Shao Shiwei has heard similar viewpoints many times in his exchanges with police officers, prosecutors, and judges handling cases across the country.

The question remains: does an account being frozen equate to the perpetrator knowing they received illicit funds? Can an unexplained account freeze directly influence subsequent transactions, thus establishing the perpetrator's subjective knowledge of aiding and abetting the crime? The conclusion is: an account freeze can be one piece of evidence for determining subjective knowledge, but the mere fact that it was previously frozen cannot be used to directly presume that the perpetrator knew others were using the internet to commit crimes. To determine whether such a presumption holds, we must first answer a frequently overlooked question: what information did the perpetrator obtain when their account was frozen or restricted? 1. The Subjective Knowledge Rule for Aiding and Abetting: Can Continuing Transactions After Account Restriction Presume Knowledge?

If an account continues to trade after being restricted due to suspected fraud, this can be used as a presumption of subjective knowledge for the crime of aiding and abetting fraud, but a comprehensive judgment is necessary, and contrary evidence is allowed to overturn it.

Article 11, Paragraph 1 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases of Illegally Using Information Networks and Assisting Information Network Crimes" (Fa Shi [2019] No. 15) stipulates that if a person continues to provide technical support or assistance after being notified by the regulatory department, it can be presumed that he or she was aware that others were using information networks to commit crimes, unless there is contrary evidence.

Article 5, Paragraph 2, Item (ii) of the "Opinions of the Supreme People's Court, the Supreme People's Procuratorate, and the Ministry of Public Security on Issues Concerning the Handling of Criminal Cases of Assisting Cybercrime" (Fa Fa [2025] No. 12) further clarifies that if a person continues to engage in related activities after being subject to restrictions or service suspension by financial institutions due to fraud or other abnormal circumstances, this can be used as evidence of subjective knowledge in determining the crime of assisting cybercrime. This article also requires a comprehensive assessment considering factors such as transaction method, number of transactions, illegal profits, past experience, professional identity, and whether supervision was evaded. So, does continuing to buy and sell virtual currency after a bank card has been frozen necessarily constitute subjective knowledge? The answer is no. The above rules stipulate that presumptions are possible, not automatic determinations; they specify that restrictive measures are taken due to abnormal circumstances such as fraud, not that all judicial freezes, bank risk control, and non-counter restrictions have the same evidentiary significance. Therefore, specific cases still require examination of why the account was frozen, whether the perpetrator knew the reason for the freeze, what the relevant authorities informed them of, and whether there was a substantial connection between the previous account abnormalities and subsequent OTC transactions. 2. The key to presuming subjective knowledge in the crime of aiding and abetting fraud: What exactly was the perpetrator informed when the account was frozen? In cases of aiding and abetting fraud involving virtual currency transactions, the prosecution's presumption of subjective knowledge is usually based on the perpetrator's previous experience of having their account frozen. However, the amount of information obtained by different people varies greatly behind the phrase "had been frozen." It is logically untenable to presume that all people whose accounts have been frozen "should have known." Many investigators assume that a frozen account means the perpetrator has been explicitly informed of receiving illicit funds. However, the reality is far more complex. Most people involved in cryptocurrency trading experience the following when their accounts are frozen: their bank card suddenly becomes unusable, they call customer service, and are told it's a "judicial freeze." The bank won't tell you which agency froze it, why, or which funds are involved. Some can't even find the contact information for the freezing authority. They wait for it to automatically unfreeze on time, and no one contacts them; nothing happens. Another, even more easily overlooked, situation is when the previous account freeze had absolutely nothing to do with cryptocurrency trading. This includes everyday bank transfers being frozen, payments for goods in foreign trade being frozen, and the bank's own anti-money laundering risk control system being mistakenly triggered—all very common in practice. Those who have experienced this "frozen for months, automatically unfrozen, and no one contacting them" situation understand account freezing as something similar to bank risk control limits—just wait and see. Asking them to conclude that "they might receive illicit funds in future OTC transactions" is completely unthinkable.

3. The Spectrum of Informed Parties' Account Freezing in Assisting Fraud Cases: How Do Seven Levels of Information Affect Subjective Knowledge?

Based on his experience handling cases involving virtual currencies, Attorney Shao divides the information actually obtained by the perpetrator after an account is frozen into seven levels, summarized as the "spectrum of informed parties' knowledge of account freezing."

Level 1: Pure Freezing, Zero Information. The bank informs the perpetrator of a "judicial freeze," but nothing else is known—they don't know which entity froze it, why it was frozen, or which transaction it's related to. Even after the freeze expires, no one contacts them. The only fact the perpetrator can confirm from this experience is "my account was frozen," and nothing else. This is the most common scenario.

The second tier: The perpetrator proactively contacted the freezing authority but received no substantial information. Being cautious, the perpetrator located the freezing authority through the bank and called to inquire. The investigators only vaguely stated, "The case is under investigation, and it's inconvenient to disclose," or requested materials explaining the source of the funds, never revealing the specific reason for the freeze. Despite making an effort to understand, the actual amount of information obtained was essentially no different from the first tier. The third tier: The perpetrator was verbally informed of the general direction, but received no written documentation. Investigators briefly mentioned over the phone or in person, such as "Your account received funds related to telecom fraud" or "Your money is involved in an online gambling case," but provided no written materials, nor clarified which transaction or counterparty it pertained to. Another common explanation was, "To unfreeze, you need to compensate the victims." While the perpetrator was confused, they objectively received a signal: the freeze was related to some crime, and the money in the account might be related to the victims. The information in this stage is a step up from the previous two, but the specific details are still vague. The fourth stage: A formal statement or interview has been taken, and the content involves the reason for the freeze. The public security organs require cooperation in taking a statement or conducting a face-to-face interview. The content of the interview involves the reason for the freeze and related transactions, but the level of detail varies greatly—some statements only state "your account received funds involved in the case," but it's still unclear which specific transaction; others are more detailed, pointing out several suspicious deposits within a certain time period, and even mentioning specific counterparties. At this stage, it's no longer possible to simply say "I don't know anything," but how much one knows depends on the content of the statement. The fifth stage: A written notification or "Risk Warning Letter" has been received. The public security organs have issued a formal written document, clearly stating the reason for the freeze and the details of the funds involved, and some even require a signature. At this stage, with written materials in hand, it's very difficult to say "I don't know why it was frozen." Sixth Tier: Specific transactions, specific counterparties, and specific sources of illicit funds are explicitly stated. The investigating authorities clearly inform you: In a certain transaction with a certain person, the money they paid you was illicit funds transferred from a victim in a certain case, and the amount involved is [amount missing]. Being informed to this extent makes it very difficult to say "I don't know." Seventh Tier: Criminal investigations have been initiated, and even coercive measures have been taken against you. It's not just that your account was frozen; you were summoned, released on bail, or even briefly detained. Later, due to insufficient evidence or minor offenses, the case was ultimately dropped or no prosecution was initiated. In this case, you have already gone through the entire criminal process and have the highest level of understanding of the nature of the crime involved. 4. The Boundary of Proof of Subjective Knowledge in the Crime of Aiding and Abetting: Why Can't the Experience of Account Freezing Replace the Content of Knowledge? The experience of account freezing only strengthens the evidence of subjective knowledge in the crime of aiding and abetting fraud when it is linked to the information provided, subsequent transactions, and unusual characteristics. The above seven levels are not absolute dividing lines; in practice, specific situations may fall between any two levels. However, this spectrum illustrates one thing: the amount of information obtained by different perpetrators during their previous involvement varies greatly. The difference between "knowing nothing" and "having been criminally investigated" is several orders of magnitude. The more specific and clear the information a perpetrator obtains from their previous experiences, the less room there is for them to claim "ignorance" when continuing transactions. Conversely, for someone who doesn't even understand why their account was frozen last time, using that experience to presume subjective knowledge of a later transaction is missing too many crucial elements. In practice, however, law enforcement agencies often lump all instances of account freezes together when pursuing prosecutions—assuming that if an account has been frozen, it means the perpetrator "should have known" they might receive illicit funds. This reasoning skips the most crucial step: what information did the perpetrator actually know? This spectrum of knowledge will be used in the following two core questions: First, if an account is frozen while the same transaction is in progress, and the perpetrator completes the transaction with a different card, can this be considered as having subjective knowledge? This depends on what information the perpetrator obtained at the time the freeze occurred and whether there is sufficient evidence to link the freeze to the current transaction; Second, between different transactions, can previous involvement in the case be transferred to subsequent new transactions? This also depends on where the perpetrator's level of knowledge on the spectrum was during the previous experience. These two scenarios involve cross-dimensional analysis from multiple perspectives. Subsequent articles in this series, "Buying and Selling Virtual Currency Suspected of Assisting Credit Fraud: Can Receiving Payments After Card Freezing Be Considered Subjective Knowledge?" and "If a Virtual Currency Transaction Was Previously Involved in a Case, Can Subsequent Transactions Be Presumed to Indicate Knowledge of Assisting Credit Fraud?", will discuss these scenarios in detail.

Author: Lu Zhilin

Between 2025 and 2026, the boundary between the traditional securities market and the crypto asset market is undergoing structural changes:

Stocks such as Apple, Nvidia, and Tesla, which have long been listed on the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, are beginning to appear on the blockchain in the form of tokens, possessing characteristics such as 24/7 trading, self-custodied wallet storage, and even use as collateral for DeFi protocols.

This trend is often referred to as "Traditional Finance Onchain," and is one of the most active areas of intersection between the crypto industry and traditional finance. "Stock tokenization" is not a single product form, but rather corresponds to multiple technological paths and business models.

While Robinhood, Ondo Finance, Kraken's xStocks, Hyperliquid, and Coinbase are often discussed together, their underlying mechanisms, compliance structures, and risk exposures differ significantly. This article attempts to systematically outline two aspects: the technical implementation path of stock tokenization; and the models adopted by major platforms, the scope of covered assets, and their corresponding risk characteristics. It also focuses on analyzing the prevalent issue of redemption capacity in the industry.

Technical Path:

How Stock Tokenization is Implemented

To understand the differences between different platforms, it is necessary to first clarify the technical process of converting a stock from a traditional exchange record into an on-chain token. Currently, there are three main implementation paths in the industry.

  • Path 1: Indirect Tokenization (Synthetic Exposure Model)

This is the method currently adopted by most platforms. Its core mechanism is that an issuing entity—usually a special purpose vehicle (SPV) registered in offshore jurisdictions such as Jersey or the British Virgin Islands—purchases and holds the underlying shares from a regulated broker, and then issues structured notes or debt instruments linked to the stock price on-chain.

Holders obtain a claim on the issuing entity, not the stock itself, and do not have voting rights; dividends are usually reflected indirectly through token rebasing mechanisms or by airdropping after purchasing more underlying shares.

Ondo Finance, Kraken's xStocks (issued by Backed), and Robinhood's Stock Tokens all follow this path. Its advantages lie in fewer compliance issues and faster expansion of target assets; the trade-off is that investor equity is structurally weaker than direct shareholding—once the issuing entity enters liquidation proceedings, token holders have a lower priority in receiving compensation than direct shareholders.

  • Path Two: Direct Tokenization (Issuer-Led Model)

This path attempts to natively record the stock itself on the blockchain, theoretically giving token holders rights equivalent to traditional shareholders, including voting rights and cash dividends.

This path attempts to natively record the stock itself on the blockchain, theoretically giving token holders rights equivalent to traditional shareholders, including voting rights and cash dividends.

This path presents significantly higher technical and compliance hurdles. Coinbase is currently making rapid progress with its B20 standard tokenized stock, launched on the Base blockchain. The underlying shares are held in a 1:1 ratio by a regulated custodian and broker Alpaca, with investor rights protected through a bankruptcy-isolated trust structure. Coinbase defines it as "on-chain representation of actual stock equity" rather than a derivative, and supports automatic dividends. Ondo is also moving in this direction, acquiring SEC-registered broker Oasis Pro in October 2025 to strengthen its US compliance license.

  • Path 3: Purely Synthetic Perpetual Contracts Not Involving Underlying Asset Holding

Represented by Hyperliquid's HIP-3 mechanism, this model does not involve the purchase and custody of underlying stocks. It relies entirely on oracle price data to drive contract settlement and has no custody relationship with real stocks. This will be discussed in detail below.

Three paths constitute a risk spectrum: At one end is a synthetic contract like Hyperliquid, completely detached from the underlying asset and only tracking its price; in the middle are indirect models like Ondo, xStocks, and Robinhood, where debt securities are issued by SPVs; and at the other end is Coinbase's ongoing direct tokenization initiative, aiming to grant token holders substantial shareholder rights. Although collectively referred to as "tokenized stocks," the actual rights and benefits investors receive differ significantly across these paths, which is a prerequisite for evaluating the products of various platforms.

Main Platform Overview

  • Robinhood

Robinhood will launch Stock Tokens for European users on Arbitrum in mid-2025, covering over 200 US stock derivatives including Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and Nvidia, as well as derivatives of equity in unlisted companies such as OpenAI and SpaceX. Main Platform Overview

  • Robinhood will launch Stock Tokens for European users on Arbitrum in mid-2025, covering over 200 US stock derivatives including Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and Nvidia, as well as derivatives of equity in unlisted companies such as OpenAI and SpaceX. The nature of these products is closer to Contracts for Dif These tokens are restricted to circulation within Robinhood's own app and wallet system, and are not open for withdrawal to external wallets. The free circulation characteristics brought by blockchain are not fully utilized in this product. xStocks (Kraken + Backed) is currently a publicly traded token product with relatively high liquidity. xStocks, issued by Backed Finance (regulated under the Swiss/EU compliance framework) and with trading access provided by Kraken, launched on May 22, 2025. It covered approximately 60 assets, including ETFs such as Apple, Nvidia, Tesla, GameStop, and SPY, and was issued in the form of Solana SPL tokens. It also supports multiple chains including Ethereum, TON, and Ink. A key difference from Robinhood is that xStocks allows withdrawals to self-custodied wallets, enabling truly free on-chain trading. Within a year of its launch, the number of assets expanded to 100, with a cumulative trading volume exceeding $25 billion. The official plan is to expand to over 500 assets by the end of 2026, and an agreement has been signed with the London Stock Exchange Group to include the 100 largest UK stocks by market capitalization in the xStocks system, covering more than 110 countries and regions. It should be noted that xStocks also does not grant voting rights to holders and is currently not open to users in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Ondo Global Markets is positioned as infrastructure rather than a trading terminal. Compared to xStocks, which focuses on the breadth of underlying assets, Ondo's product design places greater emphasis on liquidity depth and the integrity of its compliance architecture. In addition to the aforementioned instant minting/burning mechanism, Ondo introduces several additional safeguards in its compliance structure: Tokens are issued through an offshore SPV; the board of directors has independent directors; assets and accounts are completely segregated from Ondo Finance's parent company to achieve bankruptcy remoteness; an independent third party, Ankura Trust, acts as a guarantor, holding first-priority collateral rights to the underlying collateral; and the issuer is required to continuously maintain over-collateralization. In 2026, Ondo partnered with Broadridge to open proxy voting and company document access functions to holders of over 250 tokenized stocks and ETFs on its platform—although the tokens themselves do not directly grant shareholder rights, the platform will exercise these rights on behalf of users based on their voting preferences. Ondo Global Markets currently boasts a scale exceeding $700 million, primarily targeting non-US investors. It has already launched on Ethereum and BNB Chain, plans to expand to Solana, and supports cross-chain transfers of over 100 tokenized stocks through the Ondo Bridge launched by LayerZero. Hyperliquid (HIP-3) is a synthetic exposure model that does not rely on underlying asset holdings. Hyperliquid's approach differs fundamentally from the aforementioned companies. Strictly speaking, it doesn't belong to "stock tokenization," but rather to "synthetic exposure to stock prices." Its HIP-3 mechanism allows third-party builders who meet the staking threshold to deploy perpetual contract markets on Hyperliquid's underlying liquidation engine without requiring platform approval for each transaction. Builders only need to define the oracle price feed and contract parameters. Currently, the largest deployment within this system is TradeXYZ. Its XYZ100 contract, which tracks the "Market Capitalization Weighted Index of 100 Large Non-Financial Companies Listed on US Exchanges," achieved a daily trading volume of $72 million within two weeks of its launch, and its current monthly trading volume has reached billions of dollars. The total open interest of RWA perpetual contracts within the entire HIP-3 system once exceeded $2.6 billion, with TradeXYZ accounting for more than four-fifths. This mechanism does not involve underlying stocks, dividends, or redemption arrangements. The transaction is essentially a contract driven by oracle prices and settled in stablecoins or HYPE, similar in essence to contracts for difference (CFDs) in traditional finance, only the matching system has been changed to a permissionless on-chain architecture. This design also raises significant regulatory applicability issues: when the same price exposure is provided by an anonymous builder holding staked tokens, rather than by a registered exchange regulated by the SEC or CFTC, the current regulatory registration path lacks a clear applicable anchor. Coinbase is currently the closest tokenization path to actual equity. Coinbase will launch B20 standard tokenized US stocks in June 2026, with initial tokens including Nvidia, Apple, Meta, and Alphabet. Deployed on its own Layer 2 network, Base, and operating under the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) regulatory rules, it is open to qualified overseas investors. A key difference from the aforementioned platforms is that Coinbase emphasizes that this product is not a derivative. The underlying shares are held 1:1 by the regulated custodian broker Alpaca, protecting investor rights through a bankruptcy-isolated trust structure, supporting automatic dividends, and planning to gradually open up stock lending, collateralized financing, and direct transfers between users. Coinbase also integrates with Chainlink to provide real-time price data for the tokens, allowing tokenized Nvidia shares to be directly used as collateral for the Aave lending protocol. According to RWA.xyz data, the total market capitalization of the tokenized stock sector is currently about $2.48 billion, with a monthly transaction volume of $27.28 billion and more than 2.1 million holders. Coinbase's entry will, to some extent, push the industry as a whole toward "getting closer to actual equity".

    • Other Participants


    Binance launched bStocks on June 11, 2026; Bitget simultaneously launched two product lines—rToken, covering more than 500 US stock ETFs, supporting 24/7 trading and integrating contract leverage and wealth management functions, and Stock+, targeting actual stock holding needs, covering more than 10,000 US stocks and ETFs and supporting the exercise of shareholder rights. By 2026, major leading cryptocurrency exchanges have largely completed their product deployment in this sector. The core issue: Can the tokens truly be redeemed? The above analysis mainly focuses on product design and the scope of target coverage, but for investors, a more substantial question is: can the tokens they hold be redeemed for their corresponding real value under conditions of needing to liquidate or extreme market conditions? This issue can be broken down into three levels according to risk levels. The first layer: Pure contract model, represented by Hyperliquid HIP-3, essentially lacks a "redemption" stage. Since this model does not involve actual holding of the underlying stock, users trade a price-tracking contract, with profits and losses settled in stablecoins or HYPE, without involving redemption arrangements for the underlying assets. The core risk of this type of product is not redemption capability, but the reliability of the oracle pricing and liquidation mechanism. A relevant case emerged in the first half of 2026: a perpetual contract referencing SK Hynix's stock price triggered a 19% price drop on a platform with low liquidity, leading to a chain of forced liquidations. The operator subsequently agreed to compensate the affected users. This case demonstrates that when thin liquidity, high leverage, and indirect price feeds combine, prices themselves are at risk of distortion. The actual liquidation price largely depends on market depth at the time, rather than the theoretical price. The second layer: For most platforms, such as Ondo, xStocks, and Robinhood, redemption is essentially a commitment made by the issuer, rather than an automated mechanism with enforceable power. These platforms generally use a Proof of Reserve (PoR) mechanism, establishing a liquidity pool and regularly disclosing holdings to prove that on-chain tokens are pegged 1:1 to the underlying stock. Ondo further incorporates a bankruptcy remote structure and a third-party guarantee agent, Ankura Trust. However, PoR is essentially a periodic snapshot provided by the issuer itself, not a real-time audit continuously performed by an independent third party. Investors cannot verify the complete correspondence between the tokens circulating on the chain and the underlying holdings at any given time. More importantly, there is the issue of legal hierarchy: The legal status of holders of such tokens is that of creditors of the issuing SPV, not shareholders of the underlying shares. If the issuing entity enters liquidation or bankruptcy proceedings, the actual amount of compensation received by token holders depends on their priority of repayment in the bankruptcy proceedings, rather than directly receiving equivalent shares. Industry analysts generally recommend verifying three elements before investing: the issuer's qualifications, verifiable asset custody certificates, and specific redemption mechanism terms. If these cannot be verified, the product held is essentially just a price tracking tool, not an equity certificate equivalent to stocks. The third layer: Models like Coinbase, where the underlying shares are held by licensed custodian entities and a bankruptcy-remote trust structure, carry relatively lower risk. Because the underlying assets are held in custody by regulated brokerage entities such as Alpaca, token holders' claims to the underlying assets are theoretically more direct, and the credibility of redemption is closer to that of traditional securities accounts. However, it should be noted that this approach is currently limited in scale and has been online for a short time. It has not yet undergone significant market stress testing, and its reliability is still mainly based on theoretical design, without sufficient empirical verification. Furthermore, liquidity during non-trading hours is a common problem faced by all models. One of the core selling points of tokenized stocks is 24/7 tradability, but the underlying stock itself is limited by the fixed opening hours of traditional exchanges. Outside of regular trading hours, tokenized products can only rely on their own on-chain market depth, rather than markets with deep liquidity like the NYSE or Nasdaq. The general consensus in the industry is that liquidity shortages during non-trading hours are the norm, bid-ask spreads tend to widen, and it is not uncommon for token prices to deviate from the underlying spot price—orders can be submitted, but this does not guarantee a fair transaction price. In other words, the "24/7 trading" feature comes at the cost of liquidity depth. It's also important to note that these products are generally not included in traditional securities investor protection systems. In the United States, securities assets in regulated brokerage accounts are covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC), and investors can receive compensation in the event of brokerage bankruptcy. However, tokenized stock holders are not covered by corresponding deposit insurance or investor protection funds in most jurisdictions. This means that if the issuer encounters operational problems, investors can primarily rely on the issuer's own asset segregation design and legal structure, rather than external mandatory protection mechanisms. Based on the above three levels, it can be concluded that the question of "whether it can truly be redeemed" currently depends more on trust in the issuer than on institutional guarantees. Mechanisms such as reserve certificates, bankruptcy remote structures, and third-party guarantees all play a role in enhancing credibility, but no single design can provide absolute certainty. This is a key factor that investors need to assess during the rapid expansion of this sector. Regulatory Progress: Framework is taking shape, implementation will take time. This wave of stock tokenization is closely related to the shift in US regulatory attitudes. Since its launch in July 2025, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins' "Project Crypto" initiative has been continuously advancing the establishment of a digital asset classification framework: The explanatory document released in March 2026 categorizes crypto assets into four main types: digital goods, digital collectibles, digital instruments, and tokenized securities. It also clarifies the core criteria for determining whether a security constitutes real equity, regardless of whether it is recorded on a blockchain or in a traditional database, the registration of ownership, approval of transfer, and the actual controller of shareholder rights are crucial. Tokenized shares issued by third parties are, in most cases, only classified as synthetic exposures. On August 18, 2026, the SEC further proposed a new regulation called "Regulation Crypto Assets," aiming to establish a dedicated regulatory framework for investment contracts involving crypto assets. This includes provisions allowing startups to be exempt from registration for 12 months and limiting fundraising to no more than $5 million. As of now, this proposal is still in the public comment phase and has not yet become a formally effective rule. Overall, the industry is currently in a transitional phase where regulatory consensus is gradually forming, but specific rules have not yet been implemented: regulators have clearly recognized the legality of the tokenization mechanism itself and are actively promoting the construction of supporting compliance frameworks; however, whether products using synthetic exposure models such as Ondo, xStocks, and Robinhood should be regulated according to the registration and disclosure standards of traditional securities remains undefined. This regulatory vacuum is a key factor that has enabled related platforms to rapidly expand and seize market share over the past year. Conclusions can be summarized as follows: First, "tokenized stocks" are not a single product type; investors must clarify the specific form of their holdings before investing. The risk structures of these three types of contracts differ fundamentally: Hyperliquid-style synthetic contracts that don't involve any underlying assets, Ondo, xStocks, and Robinhood-style debt securities issued by SPVs, and Coinbase's direct tokenization aimed at mimicking actual equity. Secondly, achieving both deep liquidity and complete compliance is currently difficult. xStocks has established relatively deep liquidity through its first-mover advantage and multi-platform alliances; Ondo has built trust at the institutional level through its instant minting/burning mechanism and more complete bankruptcy remoteness structure; Coinbase has chosen a path with higher compliance thresholds but a long-term positioning closer to actual equity. It is currently difficult to determine which path will ultimately dominate the market. Third, the implementation of regulatory rules will likely lag behind the speed of product expansion. The SEC's relevant framework is still in the proposal stage, while platforms have already substantially expanded their market share. This time lag constitutes both a first-mover advantage and the most significant source of uncertainty. Fourth, repayment capacity currently relies primarily on trust mechanisms rather than institutional guarantees. Except for a few platforms using physical custody, the repayment of most tokenized equity products is essentially a promise made by the issuer, rather than a readily verifiable and enforceable institutional arrangement—this is as important in investment decisions as the number of targets covered or the completeness of the on-chain ecosystem. The practice of stock tokenization, in essence, challenges the long-standing clearing, custody, and voting rights system of the traditional securities market with the technological efficiency of blockchain. In terms of technical feasibility, this path has been initially validated; however, whether it can be truly established in terms of institutional design and market trust remains to be seen. On September 5th, the National Sheriffs' Association (NSA) announced that it was withdrawing its opposition to the CLARITY Act, the cryptocurrency market structure bill, and becoming "neutral." In a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, the NSA stated that given the extensive work already done by Congress, the government, and industry stakeholders on the legal, regulatory, and enforcement issues addressed by the bill, the organization decided to "step back and allow the legislative process to continue" to establish a clear, effective, and urgently needed regulatory framework.

Previously, the NSA opposed certain provisions in the bill concerning regulatory exemptions for cryptocurrency mixers, arguing that such provisions could weaken law enforcement's ability to track on-chain transactions and recover victims' funds. The NSA also criticized the CLARITY Act for "protecting the crypto industry, not the public." Currently, the US Senate plans to proceed with a procedural vote on the CLARITY Act on September 15. While the bill has made progress with the Senate Agriculture and Banking Committees, issues such as stablecoin rewards, tokenized stocks, and potential conflicts of interest with the Trump family remain controversial.

On September 5, Canadian Prime Minister Carney's plan to build artificial intelligence infrastructure is facing local resistance. Canada, with its lower temperatures, abundant energy resources, and ample land, is seen as an alternative for Silicon Valley companies to build data centers, but a growing number of communities are opposing the expansion of server facilities.

Oakville, Ontario, and Rockieville, Alberta, have suspended data center projects for a year, and Manitoba Premier Wabue Keeneau also rejected a data center construction plan near Winnipeg. Some residents are concerned about the high power consumption and noise levels of large data centers, and the potential for driving up electricity prices. The Carney government believes that data center construction helps enhance Canada's digital sovereignty and released a framework on Thursday requiring projects to create long-term local benefits, reduce environmental impact, and avoid passing on electricity costs to residents. Tech companies such as Amazon, Meta, and Anthropic have signed the relevant principles. Canada currently has five large data centers in operation, with another 159 projects announced or under construction. The government hopes to address community concerns about the distribution of energy, environmental, and economic benefits while promoting the development of AI infrastructure. ZeroBytes previously attacked the French National Tax Service (DGFiP), and officials confirmed that at least 678,000 individuals and businesses were affected, including names, tax information, and contact details. ZeroBytes had previously claimed to have sold some of the stolen tax data to buyers. Recently, fake DGFiP paper mail targeting Crypto holders has also appeared in France. Scammers use the pretext of DAC8 digital asset declaration to lure recipients into scanning QR codes to phishing websites and steal wallet information. ▌Can Bitcoin Still Be Called "Digital Gold" During Geopolitical Crises?

Every geopolitical crisis causes gold prices to rise while Bitcoin prices plummet. After six tests, the claim of "digital gold" has never been supported by data. Countries hoard gold but exclude Bitcoin from their reserves. For investors, Bitcoin exhibits asymmetry: it falls with stocks but does not rise with them. Three structural asymmetries prevent Bitcoin from achieving safe-haven status: an oversupply of derivatives (market structure), the dominance of leveraged traders (participant composition), and a lack of repeatable behavioral records (behavioral accumulation).

Bitcoin is not a safe-haven asset, but it is a "crisis-useful asset," which can indeed function when borders are closed and banks fail. If these three asymmetries are reduced, Bitcoin may no longer be a replica of gold but rather a completely new "next-generation gold."

Generational shifts and the widespread application of algorithms are key factors that could accelerate this process.

data.title: Fomo earns 1.2 million a day, so why are the two major exchanges nervous?
data.description: On September 3rd, data from on-chain data agency SolanaFloor showed that social trading app Fomo's daily revenue reached $1.2 million, setting a new record. While this figure doesn't rank in the top five within the entire crypto industry, what unsettles the wallet teams at Binance and OKX isn't the number itself, but rather the underlying logic that even these two established exchanges failed to replicate. What's truly interesting is that Fomo itself doesn't shy away from the fact that its products have shortcomings, even the founders don't deny them. In an interview, co-founder Se Yong Park frankly admitted that the web version of Fomo is "a bit lacking in functionality," remaining at the level it was at launch, and the team currently doesn't have the resources to polish it—but web version traffic already accounts for about 25% of the platform's total traffic, an entry point that even the team admits is "lacking in quality." However, this hasn't stopped it from surging along its growth curve. According to data from Dune Analytics, Fomo's trading bot has achieved the number one position in trading volume and market share in the meme trading sector; Se Yong revealed in an interview that the platform's users have grown to 1.3 million, and are still adding 30,000 net users every day. Looking back, according to statistics from the on-chain data platform DeFiLlama, Fomo set a record of $2.64 million in protocol revenue for a single week on August 8th, breaking its own weekly revenue record three times within a month, with annualized revenue reaching $29.22 million at one point; on August 16th, its single-day protocol revenue even surpassed that of the established derivatives platform Hyperliquid; on August 21st, Fomo briefly entered the top three of the US financial application rankings, surpassing Cash App and the prediction market Kalshi, and is currently stable within the top 15. Behind this is a $75 million Series B funding round led by Silicon Valley veteran Index Ventures, with participation from established venture capital firm Union Square Ventures (USV). This round valued the company, founded by three former employees of the decentralized exchange dYdX, at $550 million, bringing its total disclosed equity funding to approximately $94 million. What truly worries Binance and OKX isn't user volume, but rather the workflow Fomo has established: information flow → trading → creator revenue sharing. When a user buys a token on Fomo, they can casually write a short "why they bought it" thesis. If someone sees this purchase record and follows suit, the original author receives a portion of the transaction fees generated (Creator Revenue). According to co-founder Se Yong Park, the Trader Rewards program alone disbursed nearly $2 million in a single week at the end of August. This means that even a regular account with only a few hundred followers can earn a share of this money if their trades are copied, without having to accumulate tens of thousands of followers, accept advertisements, or do rebates as in the past. What are Binance and OKX in such a hurry for? According to KOL CryptoBraveHQ (@cryptobraveHQ), OKX has held multiple internal meetings, hoping to replicate Fomo's functionality in its own wallet. He also believes that exchange wallets developed by Chinese teams generally lack a natural understanding of overseas "leading" communities and the original culture of Western memes, a gap that cannot be bridged with a single product iteration. Binance, on the other hand, has absolutely no intention of following Fomo's approach. It's sticking to its strongest strategy—first, attract users by creating a profit-making effect through assets, then addressing product experience gaps later. On September 2nd, Binance Alpha just added the meme coin, FLORD. According to our observations, this coin quickly gained popularity within days of its launch, a perfect example of Binance's consistent approach on BNB Chain—first create a profit story to attract attention, then address the technology and product development later. This is also the most crucial point of contention in this competition: Binance and OKX hold the moat of the right to issue assets—the power to decide which assets are seen first; while Fomo is leveraging the power of information—the power to be closest to the trading decision. For the past decade, exchanges have been able to capture the vast majority of trading volume simply by leveraging the former, because on-chain information is scattered across countless Telegram groups and X (formerly Twitter) KOLs, and exchanges don't need to consolidate it. Now, Fomo packages these scattered information flows, real positions, and revenue sharing mechanisms into a single product, essentially bypassing the issuance of rights and directly building a new entry point in the "attention-trading" link. It's worth noting that this competition is unlikely to simply boil down to a choice between "Fomo or exchange wallets." Another slightly different approach in the market comes from Coinbase's Base ecosystem—it doesn't compete on meme culture or create wealth through asset issuance, but instead focuses on making wallets compliant payments, fiat currency gateways, and on-chain financial infrastructure. In other words, the wallet race is shifting from a single competition of "who has the most comprehensive functions" to several parallel moats of "who controls the culture, who controls the assets, and who controls the compliant infrastructure." The battle between exchange wallets and Fomo is just one of the most direct lines of attack. It's not just exchanges that are anxious. This battle for trading gateways isn't limited to Binance and OKX alone. According to Se Yong Park in an interview, just a week before this interview, Pump.fun, a long-established meme coin launch platform, was reported to be poaching top traders from the Fomo platform with hefty sums. In Fomo's model, a trader's personal account is itself an asset; whoever's positions are seen and followed by more people receives a larger share of the creator's revenue, making top traders a scarce resource that various platforms are vying for. Se Yong's response to this was quite restrained: competition is a good thing; Fomo's goal is to expand the entire "pie," rather than confining itself to the existing crypto Twitter (CT) circle to grab users. According to him, Fomo doesn't even want to define itself as a "crypto company," but rather wants to become a social financial platform where "anything can be traded." This statement sounds like public relations rhetoric, but considering its already planned community feature (Clans)—where users can team up to participate in leaderboard battles, co-build funding pools, and even receive airdrops from projects under the community name—it's clear that Fomo isn't just targeting Binance and OKX wallet users, but also the top traders held by platforms like Pump.fun. The previous revenue-sharing model, which directly linked "trading recommendations" to trading volume for profit sharing, wasn't invented by Fomo. The established social trading platform eToro's Popular Investor program adopted a similar logic years ago: bloggers' monthly income is linked to their AUC (Amount Under Traded), with higher tiers receiving a larger share. This mechanism has indeed cultivated a group of top trading bloggers, but it has also been accompanied by long-standing controversy—when income is directly tied to "how many people follow their trades," do bloggers have an incentive to increase their positions and create more sensational narratives to attract more followers? This question has been debated for over a decade with eToro: should the upper limit of a single blogger's share be limited, or should the market be allowed to weed out those who fail? There is still no unified approach in the industry. Fomo's trader rewards and creator revenue sharing essentially bring the same incentive structure onto the blockchain and into the already highly volatile MIME coin market. The leaderboards and feeds create verifiable public records of bloggers' positions and profits/losses, making them harder to fake than DEX leaderboards which are easily manipulated. However, this same mechanism could also distort the "sharing trading logic" into "creating trading signals for revenue sharing." This isn't a problem Binance or OKX currently needs to worry about, but it's a question every ordinary user preparing to invest in the Fomo ecosystem should consider carefully. Fomo has not yet confirmed whether it will issue a token. A platform that just secured $75 million, is aggressively subsidizing traders and creators, has been poached by Pump.fun, and is being studied and copied by OKX—will it refine its revenue-sharing mechanism into a more transparent information pricing method, or will the pressure to grow cause "market recommendation equals profit" to "market recommendation equals manipulation"? No one can say for sure. And this answer will ultimately determine not only the valuation of an app, but also who should define the next generation of trading gateways—will it continue to be determined by exchanges through issuance rights, or will it be defined by countless ordinary users using their own positions and theses?
